passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to lament for Tyre, ‘who dwells at the gateway to the sea, merchant of the peoples on many coasts’ (verse 3). Tyre had claimed to be perfect in beauty (verse 3), and her builders perfected her beauty in the heart of the seas (verse 4).

The poem pictures Tyre as a great ship. Her planks come from the firs of Senir, her mast from a cedar of Lebanon, her oars from the oaks of Bashan, her deck is inlaid with ivory, and her sail is embroidered linen from Egypt (verses 5-7). Her rowers come from Sidon and Arvad, and soldiers from many lands hang their shields on her walls (verses 8-11). Then comes a long list of trading partners and goods, from silver, iron, tin and lead to horses, ivory, grain, wine, spices, gold and precious stones (verses 12-24). ‘The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient trade to survive, naming places from the far west to Mesopotamia and from Anatolia to Arabia. Senir is another name for Mount Hermon. Javan is the Ionian Greeks, and Tubal and Meshech were peoples of Anatolia. Dedan, Sheba and Kedar were trading peoples of Arabia. Where Tarshish lay is disputed; it was a distant western port.

Phoenician ships were famous, and the details are realistic. Purple dye, taken in tiny amounts from sea snails, was Tyre's most famous product and so costly that it became the color of royalty. Human beings appear in the list too (verse 13), traded alongside bronze vessels.
passages.later: Solomon's ships of Tarshish sailed with Hiram's fleet (1 Kings 10:22). Isaiah called Tyre ‘the bestower of crowns, whose traders are princes’ (Isaiah 23:8).
passages.asks: Tyre claimed to be perfect in beauty. Ask where your security rests in what you own or have built. And ask who is paying the cost of the things you enjoy.

passages.t: The ship sinks in the heart of the sea
passages.happening:
‘Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea’ (verse 26). All her wealth, sailors, captains, merchants and warriors will sink on the day of her downfall (verse 27).

The sailors stand on the shore and cry out bitterly. They throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes, shave their heads and put on sackcloth (verses 28-31). They lament, ‘Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?’ (verse 32). Her wares once satisfied many peoples and enriched kings (verse 33); now the coastlands are appalled, and traders hiss at her (verses 35-36).
passages.hearers:
The east wind was the hot, violent desert wind. A ship caught in it at sea could be shattered. The poem's picture is of a grand vessel overloaded with wealth, carried out into deep water by its own rowers, and broken by a storm it could not withstand.

The mourning follows known customs: dust on the head, rolling in ashes, shaved heads, sackcloth. The hissing of verse 36 was a sound of shock and horror at a ruin.
passages.later: A psalm says, ‘With a wind from the east You wrecked the ships of Tarshish’ (Psalm 48:7). Jonah's ship nearly broke apart in a storm at sea (Jonah 1:4).
passages.asks: The ship's own rowers took it into the storm. Ask where your own ambition may be carrying you into danger. And ask what you would have left if everything you trade in sank.
